hook.text: High-yield seeds need reliable water. Rainfed farmers—the majority worldwide—got far less benefit.

buildup.text: India's Green Revolution concentrated in Punjab and Haryana—regions with extensive canal and well irrigation.

discovery.text: Dry-land farmers in central and eastern India saw little yield improvement. The revolution passed them by.

twist.text: To extend benefits, governments subsidized tube wells. Groundwater pumping soared—and aquifers began declining.

climax.text: The Green Revolution's water demand created today's groundwater crisis in India, Pakistan, and China.

punchline.text: High yields need water. The bill arrives a generation later.

quiz.question: Why did rainfed farmers benefit less from the Green Revolution?
options: High-yield varieties required reliable irrigation they didn't have

details.summary: Green Revolution varieties achieve their full yield potential only with reliable irrigation, making water access the dividing line between regions that benefited from the revolution and those that did not.
details.whyItMatters: The Green Revolution's reliance on irrigation has led to massive groundwater depletion in key food-producing regions. In India's Punjab and Pakistan's Indus basin, water tables are falling at alarming rates, threatening the long-term viability of.
takeaways: Green Revolution varieties need 2-3 times more water than traditional drought-adapted crops
Irrigated land produces 40% of global food on just 20% of cultivated area
Groundwater depletion in Green Revolution heartlands threatens future food production

faq.question: Why did the Green Revolution depend so heavily on irrigation?
faq.answer: High-yielding varieties need consistent moisture throughout their growing cycle to produce maximum grain. Traditional varieties are adapted to variable rainfall, but Green Revolution varieties perform poorly under drought stress.

faq.question: What water sustainability problems has the Green Revolution created?
faq.answer: India withdraws more groundwater than any country. The Punjab water table drops over one meter per year. Pakistan's canal irrigation has salinized millions of hectares. The Ogallala Aquifer in the U.S. is being depleted for irrigated wheat and corn. These are long-term threats to food security.
